hypothesis.statement: The 502 error rate increase is caused by the new cache configuration
alternatives: Upstream service degradation coinciding with the deployment window (external failure)
Traffic spike or load pattern change overwhelming the origin
Unrelated infrastructure failure — network, DNS, or TLS certificate expiry
Database saturation cascading to the proxy/gateway layer

prior.justification: SRE literature places configuration changes as the leading cause of production incidents (~35–45% across cloud environments). A prior of 0.40 is moderately generous: it acknowledges that a newly deployed config is the most plausible single candidate when errors appear near a deployment, but leaves 0.60 mass for external failures, traffic anomalies, and pure coincidence. It is deliberately not set higher to avoid anchoring on the post-hoc temporal observation that is itself one of the evidence items.

likelihood.description: If the cache config is the cause, we expect three observable signatures: errors begin at or shortly after the config push, the error code is 502 specifically (Bad Gateway — consistent with cache misconfig blocking upstream connections to origin servers), and no other concurrent change can serve as an alternative explanation. The joint likelihood of all three is high if H is true.

evidence.description: (a) Temporal correlation: 502 error rate spike onset aligns with the cache config deployment timestamp; no elevated error rate was observed in the preceding baseline window

(b) Error code specificity: errors are precisely 502 Bad Gateway — consistent with cache misconfiguration causing invalid or refused upstream connections to origin servers; not 500 (application error), 503 (service unavailable), or 504 (gateway timeout)

(c) Isolated change window: independently verified that no other deployments, infrastructure updates, certificate rotations, or config mutations occurred during the incident window — the cache config is the sole candidate change

posterior.calculation:
Sequential update — each posterior becomes the prior for the next step.

── Step 1: Temporal correlation (e1), prior = 0.40 ──
P(H|e1) = (0.95 × 0.40) / ((0.95 × 0.40) + (0.15 × 0.60))
         = 0.3800 / (0.3800 + 0.0900)
         = 0.3800 / 0.4700
         = 0.809
         [BF₁ = 0.95 / 0.15 = 6.33 — moderate-to-strong evidence]

── Step 2: Error code specificity (e2), prior = 0.809 ──
P(H|e2) = (0.80 × 0.809) / ((0.80 × 0.809) + (0.25 × 0.191))
         = 0.6472 / (0.6472 + 0.04775)
         = 0.6472 / 0.69495
         = 0.931
         [BF₂ = 0.80 / 0.25 = 3.20 — moderate evidence]

── Step 3: Isolated change window (e3), prior = 0.931 ──
P(H|e3) = (0.90 × 0.931) / ((0.90 × 0.931) + (0.25 × 0.069))
         = 0.8379 / (0.8379 + 0.01725)
         = 0.8379 / 0.85515
         = 0.980
         [BF₃ = 0.90 / 0.25 = 3.60 — moderate evidence]

── Combined Bayes Factor ──
BF_combined = BF₁ × BF₂ × BF₃ = 6.33 × 3.20 × 3.60 = 72.9
(Overwhelmingly strong; BF > 30 = 'very strong' by Kass-Raftery scale)

sensitivity.note: Skeptical prior (0.20): posterior converges to 0.948. Generous prior (0.60): posterior reaches 0.991. The conclusion is robust to prior uncertainty — even the most skeptical starting point yields >94% posterior after all three evidence items. The combined BF of 72.9 dominates the prior.
